why: the output-Dataset author surface (ADR 0028), pinned so the Python and Go SDKs AGREE rather than each passing a check against its own docs. A Method pushes to its third parameter at whatever granularity it likes; this file fixes, for each granularity, the units in and the ordered records out. Each side selects the body named by `case` and drives it through its real engine in inline mode (no object store), then compares the run's `results` to `expected`. The peers assert THIS file: runtime/go/engine/output_dataset_conformance_test.go and tests/test_output_dataset_conformance.py.

covers.one-per-unit: the ordinary 1->1: push one record per Unit, in input order
covers.one-per-three: 1->0-or-1 keyed on the Unit's index: push {i: index} when index%3==0 — proves the granularity is the author's, no flag
covers.n-per-unit: 1->N and 1->0 in one Batch: push `value` records for a Unit whose value is N; a Unit with value 0 pushes nothing and does not fail
covers.none-for-a-unit: a Unit may push nothing and is not a failure — it just produced no rows
covers.whole-batch: one record for the WHOLE Batch, pushed AFTER the loop: it has no current Unit, so it rides the tail and folds into results after the per-Unit output

ordering: records pushed while a Unit is current attribute to it and assemble in input-index order; records pushed with no current Unit ride the tail in push order and fold in after. These cases push sequentially (no author-written goroutines), so the order is deterministic and asserted; concurrent pushes are a separate, set-not-sequence guarantee each SDK tests on its own.
